unit_label: ABFM Module D unit 4 (courseware unit 22): artificial intelligence

facts.statement: Meaning of artificial intelligence (courseware): artificial intelligence (AI) is the replication of human intelligence in computers trained to think like people and emulate human activities; it can refer to any computer that simulates mental processes common to humans, such as learning and problem solving. AI is applied across industries including banking, healthcare, surveillance and social media. Machine learning is a branch of AI, and neural networks and deep learning are in turn within machine learning. The technique of making machines perform tasks that previously needed human intelligence is AI; in its basic form, computer vision is used to conceptualise objects and a robotics process is used to control and move them. AI research studies how to create systems that respond to stimuli in a way consistent with human reflection, judgement and intention.

History of AI (courseware): the academic discipline of artificial intelligence was born in the 1950s when scientists began to investigate whether computers could process intellectual powers equal to those of humans. Alan Turing is credited with suggesting a test of machine intelligence, known as the Turing Test or imitation game, in which a machine tries to pass itself off as a human by responding to questions in a manner consistent with a person; if a person cannot tell, the machine could be judged to have the same level of intelligence. John McCarthy coined the term artificial intelligence in 1956 in preparation for a conference (the Dartmouth Conference), which helped establish AI as a separate field. Between 1956 and 1966 research was mostly theoretical.

Applicability of AI (courseware): AI has found applications in medical diagnosis, stock trading, robot control, law, remote sensing, scientific discovery and toy manufacturing. Many uses are not called AI: once something becomes valuable and common enough it is no longer thought of as AI (the courseware attributes this observation to Nick Bostrom). AI algorithms decide using real-time data, combining information from sensors, remote inputs, digital data and other sources. An intellectual difficulty can be broken into pieces with a solution for each, whether a person or a computer solves it. Intelligent computer-assisted instruction is a concept in which a computer acts as a tutor that observes a student problem-solving, recognises wrong assumptions and gives guidance fitted to that pupil; a second benefit is that the learner understands mechanical thinking.

Google examples of AI (courseware, types only): RankBrain is a machine-learning search algorithm that helps process search queries, guessing the meaning of unfamiliar words by representing words as vectors that lie close together when their meaning is similar. AI Hub is a repository of plug-and-play machine learning content (pipelines, notebooks, modules) that companies can share privately and deploy. Kubeflow Pipelines orchestrate end-to-end machine learning workflows made of containerised components, so that workflows can be built, reused and deployed to production. Google Duplex uses speech recognition, a recurrent neural network and text-to-speech to hold phone conversations such as making reservations. The product details, dates and statistics are not taught.

AI in banking and finance (courseware): AI-based systems increase productivity and lower cost and allow decisions using information unavailable to human decision makers; they detect fraud and anomalies. Examples: customer service and engagement through chatbots (a high return in cost savings; they handle routine tasks such as checking balances, viewing micro statements and making fund transfers, relieving call centres and internet banking); robo-advice (understands the client financial health from data and history and recommends investments in a product class); general-purpose predictive analytics (patterns and correlations that identify unmet sales prospects, cross-selling and operational measures); cybersecurity (learning from previous threats to forecast and block attacks and monitor internal breaches); and scoring credit and direct lending (analysing traditional and non-traditional data to assess creditworthiness, even for people with a thin credit history). Ten areas of use shown: cybersecurity and fraud detection, chatbots, loan and credit decisions, tracking market trends, data collection and analysis, customer experience, risk management, regulatory compliance, predictive analytics and process automation.

Hybrid information systems (courseware): a hybrid information system (HIS) combines several AI methods, such as a fuzzy expert system, a neuro-fuzzy system and a genetic-fuzzy system. It gains the benefits of different learning approaches and overcomes the limits of each. Uses in finance: portfolio management (portfolio selection is a complicated task and an important part of the decision process) and stock market prediction (hybrid systems combine the skills of many systems and are used much more in financial prediction than single AI methods because the market is highly unpredictable).

Future scope and building blocks of AI (courseware): in AI the computer performs natural language processing (communicating in natural language), knowledge representation (storing what it hears or knows), automated reasoning (using stored knowledge to answer questions and draw conclusions) and machine learning (adapting to new circumstances and detecting patterns). AI has many subfields from the broad (learning and perception) to the narrow (playing chess, proving theorems, diagnosing disease), and draws on computer science, philosophy, psychology, neuroscience, biology, mathematics and sociology. The courseware expects AI to affect transportation (autonomous cars), manufacturing (robots alongside humans and predictive sensors), education (tools that judge student emotion and tailor learning) and customer services (assistants that understand context and book appointments).

Neural networks (courseware): artificial neural networks are highly adaptable algorithms used in supervised and unsupervised data mining. They can replace logistic regression or decision trees, or be used with them; their adaptability lets them handle continuous dependent variables as in regression. They are especially useful when there are many input variables with non-linear relationships to the target variable; the structure is stated simply by the number of nodes and hidden layers, so the analyst need not worry about non-linearities and interactions between predictors. A neural net learns from the input data without a pre-defined statistical model and with no assumptions about linearity or normality, which is why it is associated with machine learning. A flaw is that it can be hard to understand what the model is doing. To work well they need many observations, so that training, validation and test subsets can be built.

Control theory, cybernetics and language (courseware, ideas only): self-regulating feedback systems are early examples of machine behaviour (the steam engine governor, the thermostat). Norbert Wiener is regarded as a founder of control theory and cybernetics; purposeful behaviour arises from a regulatory mechanism trying to reduce error, the gap between the existing and the desired state. Contemporary control theory (stochastic optimal control) designs systems to maximise an objective function, which is close to the AI view of creating systems that act in the best possible way. Artificial intelligence developed partly to go beyond the limits of calculus and matrix algebra, using logical inference and computing to address problems of language, vision and planning. Modern linguistics and AI developed together into computational linguistics (natural language processing); language comprehension needs knowledge of the subject and the context, and knowledge representation is the study of putting knowledge in a form a computer can reason with.

Goals of AI: reasoning and knowledge (courseware): early algorithms mirrored step-by-step human reasoning; later methods handled uncertain or partial information with probability and economics. Most early algorithms suffered a combinatorial explosion: they became exponentially slower as the problem grew; humans mostly use quick intuitive judgements rather than step-by-step deduction. Knowledge representation lets programs answer questions and draw conclusions about the real world. An ontology is a set of objects, relations, concepts and attributes formally described so software agents can interpret them; upper ontologies are the broadest, and domain ontologies cover a specific area. Commonsense knowledge is the large body of facts the average person knows; it is hard to represent because it is vast and much of it is sub-symbolic and not expressed as facts. Uses of knowledge representation include content-based indexing and retrieval, scene interpretation, clinical decision support and knowledge discovery.

Rational agents, planning and learning (courseware): a rational agent is anything that makes decisions (a person, firm, machine or software); on the basis of its previous and current perceptions it takes the action expected to give the best outcome. An AI system consists of an agent and the environment in which it operates; the environment is everything outside the agent that it can sense and act on. Planning: an intelligent agent builds a representation of the current state, predicts how actions will change it and decides what maximises the utility (value) of the available options; with other agents present it must reason under uncertainty and re-evaluate. Learning: machine learning is the study of computer systems that improve themselves through experience. Unsupervised learning looks for patterns in a stream of data; supervised learning has two main forms, classification (assigning an item to a category, such as spam or not spam) and regression (learning a function that maps inputs to a numerical output); in reinforcement learning the agent is rewarded for good responses and penalised for bad ones; transfer learning applies skills learned on one problem to a different one.

Motion and manipulation (courseware): robotics uses AI for localisation (mapping the surroundings and finding where the robot is); this is simple in a contained space and harder in dynamic environments. Robots are sought after for accuracy and worker safety (hazardous environments such as aerospace, nuclear, defence and maintenance work); disadvantages include being unsuited to jobs needing creativity, adaptability or critical decision making. Motion planning reduces a movement to basic components such as joint movements; compliant motion is movement while keeping physical contact with an object.

Tools and techniques of AI (courseware): search and optimisation (many problems are solved by searching an enormous catalogue of possible answers; simple exhaustive searches become too slow, so heuristics, or rules of thumb, rank options by how likely they are to reach the goal and prune the search tree); logic (propositional logic with or and not, first-order logic with quantifiers; fuzzy logic gives a degree of truth between 0 and 1, so a vague statement such as being rich or tall can be partly true); probabilistic methods for uncertain reasoning (Bayesian networks, decision theory using utility, Markov decision processes, game theory); and classifiers and statistical learning methods (classifiers match a pattern to the closest class from labelled data; methods include decision trees, nearest neighbour, support vector machines, naive Bayes and neural networks; their success depends on the data, including its size, class distribution and noise).

AI and morality (courseware): the courseware presents three schools of thought: one holds that, with many people in extreme poverty, there is no reason to build mechanical labourers that can think independently; another that human civilisation cannot advance without machines capable of at least some independent thought; and a third, representative of society at large, that has no interest. The courseware concludes that AI machines, like other machines, follow instructions provided by human programmers, that people need to understand AI to use it well, that expert systems can help but cannot do every task, and that AI must be used judiciously lest it prove a curse rather than a boon.

payload.title: What artificial intelligence is, and how it relates to machine learning
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is the **replication of human intelligence in computers** trained to **think and act like people**: learning, problem solving and other mental processes. It is used in **banking, healthcare, surveillance and social media**.

**Nesting:** **machine learning (ML)** is a branch of AI; **neural networks** and **deep learning** sit within ML.

In basic form, AI relies on **computer vision** to **form a picture of objects** and on **robotics** to **control and move** them. AI research builds systems that **respond to stimuli** in a way consistent with **human reflection, judgement and intention**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: AI is the broad field; machine learning is the part in which systems learn from data.

self_check.prompt_text: How is machine learning related to artificial intelligence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Machine learning is a branch of AI, and neural networks and deep learning lie within it.

payload.title: A short history of AI
payload.core_explanation_md:
AI was **born as an academic field in the 1950s**, when researchers asked whether computers could match human intellectual powers.

- **Alan Turing** proposed a test of machine intelligence, the **Turing Test (imitation game)**: if a questioner **cannot tell a machine from a person** by its answers, the machine can be judged to have the same level of intelligence.
- **John McCarthy** **coined the term artificial intelligence in 1956** for a conference (the **Dartmouth Conference**) that helped make AI a **separate field**.
- **1956 to 1966:** research was **mostly theoretical**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The test judges behaviour, not how the machine works inside.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the Turing Test judge?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Whether a machine can respond in a way that a questioner cannot tell from a human.

payload.title: Where AI is applied
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Applications:** **medical diagnosis, stock trading, robot control, law, remote sensing, scientific discovery, even toy manufacturing**.

**Many uses are not called AI**: once something is **useful and common enough** it is **no longer called AI**.

AI algorithms **decide using real-time data** from **sensors, remote inputs and digital data**. A hard problem can be **broken into parts** with a solution for each.

**Intelligent computer-assisted instruction:** a computer acts as a **tutor** that **watches a student solve a problem**, **spots wrong assumptions** and **gives guidance** fitted to that pupil; the learner also **learns mechanical thinking**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Widely adopted AI tends to be absorbed into ordinary software and then stops being labelled AI.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do many uses of AI go unlabelled as AI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Once a technique is useful and common enough it is no longer thought of as AI.

payload.title: Examples of AI products from one technology company
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware gives examples of AI building blocks; the **products and statistics are not taught**, only the **types**:

| Type | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Machine-learning search algorithm (RankBrain)** | Guesses the meaning of **unfamiliar queries** by representing words as **vectors**; similar meanings lie **close together** |
| **Repository of ML content (AI Hub)** | **Plug-and-play pipelines and modules**, shared **privately** within a company and **deployed** |
| **Workflow orchestration (Kubeflow Pipelines)** | End-to-end ML workflows built from **containerised components**; **built, reused and deployed** to production |
| **Voice assistant (Duplex)** | **Speech recognition, a recurrent neural network and text-to-speech** to hold **phone conversations** such as bookings |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: These are illustrations of how machine learning is packaged into services.

self_check.prompt_text: How does a machine-learning search algorithm handle a query it has never seen?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It represents words as vectors and guesses the meaning from words with similar vectors.

payload.title: AI in banking and finance
payload.core_explanation_md:
AI systems **raise productivity**, **cut costs**, allow decisions from **information humans cannot use** and **detect fraud and anomalies**.

| Use | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Chatbots** | **Handle routine requests** (balances, mini statements, transfers); **cost savings**; relieve call centres |
| **Robo-advice** | **Assesses client financial health** from data and history and **recommends a product class** |
| **Predictive analytics** | Finds **patterns** pointing to **unmet sales, cross-selling, operational improvements** |
| **Cybersecurity** | **Learns from past threats** to **forecast and block attacks** and **monitor internal breaches** |
| **Credit scoring and direct lending** | Uses **traditional and non-traditional data** to judge **creditworthiness**, even for **thin credit histories** |

Other areas: **loan and credit decisions, tracking market trends, risk management, regulatory compliance, process automation, customer experience**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Alternative data widens access to credit for people with no formal credit record.

self_check.prompt_text: What data can AI use for credit scoring that older methods could not?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Non-traditional data in addition to traditional data, which helps assess people with thin credit histories.

payload.title: Hybrid information systems in finance
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **hybrid information system (HIS)** **combines AI methods**; examples are **fuzzy expert**, **neuro-fuzzy** and **genetic-fuzzy** systems.

It **gains the strengths** of each learning approach and **overcomes the limits** of each.

**Uses in finance:**

- **Portfolio management**: portfolio selection is **complex** and central to decision making.
- **Stock market prediction**: markets are **highly unpredictable**, so **combined systems** are used **far more than single methods**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Combining methods spreads the weaknesses of any one technique.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are hybrid systems used in stock market prediction?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Combining several AI methods copes better with the unpredictable market than any single method.

payload.title: Building blocks of AI and where it is heading
payload.core_explanation_md:
**What the computer must do:**

- **Natural language processing**: communicate in everyday language.
- **Knowledge representation**: **store** what it knows or hears.
- **Automated reasoning**: use stored knowledge to **answer questions and draw conclusions**.
- **Machine learning**: **adapt** to new circumstances and **detect patterns**.

AI has **subfields** from the **broad** (learning, perception) to the **narrow** (chess, theorem proving, diagnosis) and draws on **computer science, philosophy, psychology, neuroscience, biology, mathematics and sociology**.

**Expected effects:** **transport** (autonomous cars), **manufacturing** (robots working alongside people; predictive sensors), **education** (tools that read student emotion and tailor learning), **customer service** (assistants that understand context and book appointments).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The four building blocks together make a system that can hear, remember, reason and improve.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four things an AI computer must be able to do.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Process natural language, represent knowledge, reason automatically and learn from data.

payload.title: Neural networks
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Artificial neural networks** are **highly adaptable** algorithms used in **supervised and unsupervised** data mining.

- Can **replace or complement logistic regression and decision trees**; handle **continuous targets** like regression.
- Excellent when there are **many inputs with non-linear relationships** to the target; the analyst need only state **nodes and hidden layers** and need not model **non-linearities or interactions**.
- **Learn from the data** with **no assumption of linearity or normality**, which is why the term **machine learning** is used.
- **Flaw:** hard to **understand what the model is doing**.
- Need **many observations** to build **training, validation and test sets**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Flexibility is bought at the price of explainability.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a main flaw of a neural network?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It can be hard to understand what the model is doing.

payload.title: Control theory, cybernetics and language
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Self-regulating feedback systems** (the **steam engine governor**, the **thermostat**) are early examples of machine behaviour. **Norbert Wiener** is regarded as a founder of **control theory and cybernetics**: purposeful behaviour comes from a mechanism trying to **reduce error**, the **gap between existing and desired state**.

**Contemporary control theory** designs systems to **maximise an objective function**, close to the AI aim of systems that **act in the best possible way**. AI grew partly to go beyond **calculus and matrix algebra**, using **logic and computing** for **language, vision and planning**.

**Language:** modern linguistics and AI grew up together as **computational linguistics (natural language processing)**. Understanding language needs **knowledge of the subject and the context**; **knowledge representation** puts knowledge in a form a computer can reason with.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A feedback loop compares the actual state with the target and acts to shrink the difference.

self_check.prompt_text: In control theory, what is the error that a regulator tries to reduce?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The gap between the existing state and the desired state.

payload.title: Reasoning, problem solving and knowledge representation
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Reasoning:** early algorithms copied **step-by-step human reasoning**; later methods handled **uncertain or partial information** using **probability and economics**.

**Combinatorial explosion:** most early algorithms became **exponentially slower** as the problem grew; people mostly use **quick, intuitive judgements** instead.

**Knowledge representation:** lets programs **answer questions and draw conclusions** about the real world.

- **Ontology:** a set of **objects, relations, concepts and attributes** formally described so that software agents can interpret them. **Upper ontologies** are the broadest; **domain ontologies** cover a specific field.
- **Commonsense knowledge:** the **vast body of facts** an average person knows; hard to represent because it is **huge** and much of it is **not stated as facts**.
- **Uses:** **indexing and retrieval by content, interpreting scenes, supporting clinical decisions, knowledge discovery**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Problems whose search space doubles with each step quickly outgrow any computer.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Computing time that grows exponentially as the problem size increases.

payload.title: Rational agents, planning and learning
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **rational agent** is anything that **makes decisions** (person, firm, machine, software) and, from its **past and present perceptions**, takes the action expected to give the **best outcome**. An AI system = **agent + environment** (everything outside the agent that it can sense and act on).

**Planning:** the agent represents the **current state**, predicts how actions **change** it and picks the action that **maximises utility**. With other agents present it must **reason under uncertainty** and **re-evaluate**.

**Learning:** systems **improve with experience**.

| Kind | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Unsupervised** | Finds **patterns** in data without labels |
| **Supervised: classification** | Assigns an item to a **category** (spam or not spam) |
| **Supervised: regression** | Learns a function mapping inputs to a **number** |
| **Reinforcement** | **Rewards** good responses, **penalises** bad ones |
| **Transfer** | Uses skills learned on **one problem** to solve **another** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Classification predicts a label; regression predicts a quantity.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between classification and regression?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Classification assigns an item to a category; regression predicts a numerical output.

payload.title: Choosing an action by expected utility, and measuring a classifier
payload.core_explanation_md:
A planning agent chooses the action with the **highest expected utility**: **expected utility = sum of (probability of each outcome x utility of that outcome)**.

A classifier can be summarised by:

- **Accuracy = correct predictions / all predictions.**
- **False alert rate = false alerts / all alerts raised.**

These measures apply the courseware idea of **maximising utility** and judging a **classifier** on how often it labels correctly; the courseware gives no worked figures.

assumptions: Probabilities of the outcomes sum to 1
Utilities are measured on one scale
common_errors: Choosing the outcome with the highest utility rather than the highest expected utility

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A rare but very valuable outcome can outweigh a likely but small one.

self_check.prompt_text: How does a rational agent choose between actions?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It picks the action with the highest expected utility.

payload.title: Motion and manipulation in robotics
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Localisation:** the robot **maps its surroundings** and **finds where it is**; easy in a **contained space**, hard in **dynamic** ones.

**Why robots are used:** **accuracy** and **worker safety** in **hazardous** settings (aerospace, nuclear, defence, maintenance).

**Limits:** poor at jobs needing **creativity, adaptability or critical decisions**.

**Motion planning** reduces a movement to **basic components such as joint movements**; **compliant motion** is movement **while keeping physical contact** with an object.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Robots shine at repeatable physical tasks but not at open-ended judgement.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Movement made while keeping physical contact with an object.

payload.title: Tools and techniques of AI
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Technique | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Search and optimisation** | Search a huge set of possible answers; **heuristics (rules of thumb)** rank options and **prune the search tree** |
| **Logic** | **Propositional** (or, and, not) and **first-order** (quantifiers); **fuzzy logic** gives a **degree of truth from 0 to 1**, so vague statements can be partly true |
| **Probabilistic methods** | **Bayesian networks**, **decision theory with utility**, **Markov decision processes**, **game theory** for **uncertain reasoning** |
| **Classifiers and statistical learning** | Match a pattern to the **closest class** from **labelled data**: **decision trees, nearest neighbour, support vector machines, naive Bayes, neural networks** |

A classifier succeeds according to the **data**: its **size, class distribution and noise**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Heuristics trade a guarantee of the best answer for speed.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a heuristic do in a search problem?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It ranks options by how likely they are to reach the goal, pruning the search tree.

payload.title: AI and morality
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware sets out **three schools of thought** on building thinking machines:

1. With **people in extreme poverty**, there is **no reason** to build **mechanical labourers that can think**.
2. **Civilisation cannot advance** without machines capable of **some independent thought**.
3. **Society at large** is **not interested**.

**Conclusions:** AI machines **follow instructions given by human programmers**; people **must understand AI** to use it well; **expert systems cannot do every task**; AI must be used **judiciously**, or it may prove **a curse rather than a boon**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Responsibility for what an AI system does rests with the people who design and deploy it.

self_check.prompt_text: Who is responsible for the instructions an AI machine follows?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The human programmers who provide them.

unresolved: This unit is the courseware general account of artificial intelligence. No banking regulation or primary technical standard applies and none was consulted. Concepts are taught at the level the courseware states them, and the courseware describes several of them loosely (for example neural networks, ontologies and logic).

The courseware gives many historical and company-specific narratives (Ktesibios, Watt, Drebbel, the Heath Robinson machine, Wiener, Ashby, Skinner and Chomsky, Panini, the Dartmouth conference and its dates, Google RankBrain with its usage percentages, Google AI Hub, Kubeflow Pipelines, Google Duplex and Hold for Me, Affirm and GiniMachine). These are narrative, were not checked and are not taught or tested as facts, apart from the two historical points the courseware makes the foundation of the subject (the imitation-game test proposed by Turing and the coining of the term artificial intelligence by McCarthy for a conference in 1956).

The courseware makes dated claims about which classifier methods are popular (for example that the naive Bayes classifier is the most extensively used learner at one company, and that k-nearest neighbour became obsolete in the 1990s). These are not taught as facts; only the existence and general nature of the methods are taught.

The courseware figure of speech "a robot that behaves like a human" and the statement that machines with human labour and talent should behave with "life, spirit and sensitivity" are not taught as technical claims.

The courseware section on morality is a brief discussion of three schools of thought; it is taught as the courseware presents it and no ethical or regulatory framework for AI in banking (for example supervisory guidance on model risk or explainability) is taught here because none is in the courseware.

The calculation items (accuracy of a classifier, cost saving from automated queries, expected utility of an action, false alert rate, fuzzy negation as one minus the degree, test-set split) are generic arithmetic applied to the courseware uses of AI in banking (chatbots with cost savings, fraud detection, decisions that maximise utility). The courseware gives no worked examples. Numbers are invented and checked in tests/content/batch-abfm-d-u04-b001.test.ts.
